summary: Huizinga worked in history, Indology, and linguistics, earning a Ph.D. from Groningen (1891–1897) and studying under Uhlenbeck, Speyer, and Kern. He taught at Amsterdam (1903–1905) and held history professorships at Groningen (1905–1915) and Leiden (1915–1941).

Madvig was a scholar of linguistics and other fields. After attending Frederiksborg Gymnasium og HF (~1817–1820), he studied at the University of Copenhagen (~1820–1826) and held a post there from ~1829 to 1879.

Van Manen worked in Tibetology and Indology. He served as second Librarian at the Adyar Library (1909–1916), Librarian at the National Library of India (1918–1921), and General Secretary of The Asiatic Society (1923–1939).

A scholar of Iranian, Central Asian, and Indological studies, von Dorn studied at Halle-Wittenberg and Leipzig (Ph.D.). He served as professor at Kharkiv (1829–1835) and the Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences (1835), and directed the Asiatic Museum (1842).

Schmeller studied at the University of Munich (~1801–1803) and later held posts at the Bavarian Cadet Corps (~1817–1826) and the Bavarian State Library (1829). He became professor of Old German language and literature at Munich in 1828 and 1846.

Vullers worked in Iranian, Central Asian, and linguistic studies. He studied at Giessen, Bonn, and Halle-Wittenberg (Ph.D.) under scholars including Schlegel, Freytag, de Sacy, and Bopp. He was a Privatdozent at Bonn (1831) and professor at Giessen (1833).
Von Orelli worked in linguistics and other fields. He held academic posts at Bündner Kantonsschule (~1819–1833), Carolinum Zürich (~1831–1833), and the University of Zurich (~1833–1849).

Rüdiger specialized in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg from 1768, later serving there as Privatdozent in 1777 and as extraordinary professor of cameral sciences in 1791.

Adelung was a linguist who studied at Kloster Berge school (~1746–1752) and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (1752). He served as a professor at Evangelisches Ratsgymnasium Erfurt (1758) and as head librarian at Dresden (1787).

Prochnow worked in linguistics and Indology after studying at the University of Greifswald (1837–1840). He served as a missionary for the Church Mission Society (1843) and director of the Gossner Evangelical Lutheran Church (~1858–1888).

De Vries, an Indologist and linguist, studied at Utrecht, Amsterdam, Lille, and Bonn (Ph.D.), learning under Caland, Schrijnen, Jacobi, and Kirfel. He served as deputy professor of Latin at Stellenbosch University in 1923.

Blumenbach worked in history, archaeology, and other fields. He studied at Ernestinum Gotha (~1765–1769), Jena (~1769–1772), and Göttingen (~1772–1775), where he subsequently held an academic post from ~1776 to 1840.
Herbart was a philosopher who studied at the University of Jena (~1794–1797). He later held a post at the University of Göttingen from ~1805 to 1841.
Kleuker worked in religious studies and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied at the University of Göttingen in 1770 and was appointed professor of theology at Kiel University in 1798.

Gildemeister worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Göttingen and Bonn under Ewald, Freytag, Lassen, and Schlegel. He taught at Bonn (Privatdozent 1839; professor 1844–1889) and Marburg (professor 1845; theological faculty 1848–1858).

Eichhorn was a scholar of religion, history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Göttingen (1770–1774) under Christian Gottlob Heyne. He served as professor of Oriental languages at Jena (1775) and professor of philosophy at Göttingen (1788).

Kosegarten worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Greifswald (1808–1812) and under Silvestre de Sacy and Chézy (1812–1814). He served as an adjunct (1814–1817) and professor (1824–1850) at Greifswald, and as professor at Jena (1817–1824).

Herder worked in philosophy, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied theology at Königsberg under Immanuel Kant. His career included teaching at the Riga Cathedral School (1764–1769), directing the Wilhelm-Ernst-Gymnasium Weimar (~1776–1803), and serving as General Superintendent of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach (1776).

Rhode specialized in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Helmstedt and earned a Ph.D. from the University of Jena (~1820–1821), having earlier served as a teacher at the Kriegsschule Berlin in 1809.

Stickel worked in linguistics and other fields. He studied at the University of Jena (1823–1826) and under Kosegarten, Hoffmann, and Silvestre de Sacy. He served as a professor at the University of Jena from 1830 to 1836.
